items.followUp: State two differences between Bohr’s atomic theory and the modern quantum mechanical model of the atom.

rubric.why: This is one key difference between the two models.
rubric.description: Rutherford’s model did not place electrons in fixed energy levels; Bohr’s model did.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that Rutherford had no fixed energy levels and contrasting it with Bohr’s shells or levels.

rubric.why: This is a second key difference, explaining how Bohr addressed a limitation of Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Bohr proposed stable permitted orbits in which electrons do not radiate energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Bohr’s permitted orbits are stable or non-radiating, or that this explains atomic stability.

modelAnswer: In Rutherford’s model, electrons could revolve around the nucleus at any distance; Bohr proposed fixed orbits or energy levels for electrons.
Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability; Bohr said electrons in permitted orbits do not radiate energy and remain stable.

items.followUp: Write the subshell electronic configuration of Mg²⁺ and state the number of electrons in its outermost shell.

rubric.why: The ion has 10 electrons after losing three electrons from a neutral aluminium atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complete correct subshell configuration.

rubric.why: The outermost occupied shell is the second shell, containing eight electrons.
rubric.description: Al³⁺ has 8 electrons in its outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct number of outermost-shell electrons.

modelAnswer: Al has atomic number 13, so Al³⁺ has 13 − 3 = 10 electrons.

items.followUp: State the modern periodic law and explain how atomic number is related to the periodic repetition of properties.

rubric.why: The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number.
rubric.description: The number of protons determines the atomic number of an element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking proton number with atomic number.

rubric.why: The periodic repetition of properties is based on increasing atomic number.
rubric.description: When elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, their properties recur periodically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that properties repeat periodically with increasing atomic number.

modelAnswer: The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number.
When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, their physical and chemical properties repeat periodically.

items.followUp: How many elements are present in the second period? Name them.

rubric.why: The first period contains two elements.
rubric.description: The number of elements in the first period is 2.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct number.

rubric.why: Both element names are required to identify the first-period elements.
rubric.description: The elements are hydrogen and helium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both elements.

items.followUp: Describe how shielding effect changes down a group and across a period.

rubric.why: Additional inner electron shells down a group increase shielding.
rubric.description: Shielding effect increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct down-group trend.

rubric.why: Across a period, added electrons enter the same main shell, so shielding changes little.
rubric.description: Shielding effect remains almost constant across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct across-period trend.

modelAnswer: Down a group, the shielding effect increases because each successive element has an additional electron shell.
Across a period, the shielding effect remains almost constant because electrons are added to the same shell.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and state what holds the ions together.

rubric.why: A chemical bond is an attractive force between particles.
rubric.description: A chemical bond is a force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a bond as a force of attraction between atoms or ions.

rubric.why: The definition should identify what the bond holds together.
rubric.description: The force holds atoms or ions together in a molecule or compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the bond holds particles together in a molecule or compound.

modelAnswer: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together in a molecule or compound.

items.followUp: What is a polar covalent bond? Give one example.

rubric.why: Equal sharing of the bonding electrons is the defining feature of a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: A non-polar covalent bond forms when the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the shared electron pair is shared equally.

rubric.why: A valid example shows a non-polar bond between identical atoms.
rubric.description: A suitable example is H₂ or Cl₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a correct example.

modelAnswer: A non-polar covalent bond is formed when the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally.

items.followUp: What is the value of absolute zero on the Kelvin scale and on the Celsius scale?

rubric.why: Absolute zero is the lowest temperature theoretically possible.
rubric.description: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the lowest possible temperature.

rubric.why: The standard Class 9 value is approximately 0 K or −273 °C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct temperature value in either standard scale.

modelAnswer: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, at which molecular motion is theoretically at its minimum.
